paragraphs.text: FUNERAL ORATION ON THE EMPRESS FLACILLA. The faithful and wise steward (for I take my opening from what has been read from the divine Gospel), whom the Lord has set over this household to give those in his charge their measure of grain in due season, did well in the time before this to condemn speech to silence. He rightly perceived the magnitude of the calamity and honored the grief with quiet. Yet I do not know how, in the present assembly, he brings speech back to the Church again, himself annulling his own verdict against it. And although I greatly admire our teacher for his understanding in many things, in this I admired him even more: that he did well to silence speech in the face of the calamity. For silence seems to me a fitting and suitable remedy for mourners, since the swelling of the soul subsides with time and [?] through quiet. For if anyone, while the grief is still

inflaming the soul, should stir up speech, the wound of sorrow will become harder to heal, scraped by the memory of painful things as if by thorns. And if it is not too bold for me to add some correction to the teacher's words, perhaps it would have been well for silence to keep its hold on us until now, so that speech, dragged toward grief, might not distress the hearers. For the time that has passed is not yet long enough to accustom the mind to what has happened [?]. The grief is still fresh in the soul, and perhaps the pain will always be fresh throughout our life. Our heart is still troubled, and like a sea lashed into waves by the storm of the calamity, it is churned up from its depths. Our thoughts still swell, boiling up at the memory of our misfortunes. When the soul is so unsteady in such a surge, how is it possible to bring speech forward on a straight course, tossed as it is by the grief of sorrow as by a hurricane? But since one must obey the one who commands, I do not know how I shall use speech. For I cannot guess the teacher's intention. Or perhaps he wishes to indulge the grief somewhat, and to stir up tears in the church with words of deeper feeling? And if this is what he intends, then in my judgment at least he does this rightly too. For surely, just as we are eager to enjoy good things, so we must also be suitably disposed toward the sorrows that befall us. Ecclesiastes too counsels this: "A time," he says, "to laugh, and a time to weep." From this we learn that we must dispose the soul in keeping with the circumstance. Are things going smoothly? It is the time to rejoice. Has brightness turned to gloom? Then it is fitting to turn cheerfulness into tears as well. For just as laughter is a sign of brightness within, so the pain in the heart is expressed by laments, and tears become, as it were, the blood of the soul's wounds. Solomon's Proverb says this too: "When the heart is glad, the face flourishes; but when the soul is in sorrow, it is downcast." So speech must by all means share the gloom of the heart's disposition. Would that it were possible to find words like those with which the great Jeremiah once lamented the calamity of the Israelites! For the present events are more deserving of those words than any of the sorrows recorded from antiquity. Grievous are the stories of Job. But why set against this evil the easily counted sufferings of a single household? Even if you go through the great and more widespread evils, earthquakes and wars and floods and chasms in the earth, these too are small when judged against the present. Why? Because the calamity of war does not strike the whole world at once; one part of it is at war while another is at peace. What else? Either a thunderbolt struck, or water flooded, or something was

swallowed up by a chasm. But the present evil is a blow to the whole world at once. It is not one nation or one city that must be mourned. Rather, it is perhaps fitting to utter the cry of Nebuchadnezzar, which he made to his subjects: "To you it is said, peoples, tribes, tongues." Or rather, allow me to add something to the Assyrian proclamation, to announce the calamity more loudly, and to say, as one might cry out on the stage: O cities and peoples, O nations and all the earth, and all of the sea that is sailed and all of it that is inhabited! O all of our world that is governed by the scepter of the empire! O all you people from every place, groan together at this grief, raise together the chorus of lament, mourn together the loss that belongs to all! Do you wish [?] that I, if I am able, should describe the loss to you as well? In our generation human nature went beyond its own bounds and surpassed its usual measures. Nature, or rather the Lord of nature, brought forth a human soul in a woman's body that surpassed almost all earlier examples of virtue. In her every virtue of body and every virtue of soul came together, and so nature showed human life an incredible marvel: how great a concourse of goods it could hold in one soul within one body. And so that the good fortune of our generation might be fully manifest to all, she was raised to the lofty throne of the empire, so that from that lofty dignity she might shine like the sun upon the whole world with the rays of her virtues. Joined in partnership of life and rule with him who by divine decree had been set over the whole world, she made his subjects blessed through herself, truly becoming, as Scripture says, a helper for him in every good thing. If it was a time for kindness, she either ran with him toward this good or even ran ahead of him; the scale stood level on either side in the weight of their benevolence. Witness to this in our speech [?] are both her former deeds, which are beyond number, and the present proclamations which we have just heard from the herald of the truth. If you look for piety, the race toward piety was common to them both. If for foresight, if for justice, if for anything else pursued for the better, everything was a contest, as each strove to surpass the other in good deeds, and neither was the loser. Each delighted equally in the other. She had as the prize of her virtue the one set over the world, while he thought authority over land and sea a small thing compared with the good fortune of having her. They gave each other equal joys, seeing each other and being seen by each other. He is such as he is (for what beauty could anyone show beyond what we see? and may what we see endure even into the life of his descendants!). But what she was cannot be shown in words, for art has left no exact likeness of her; and even if something of her exists in paintings or in sculptures, it all falls short of the truth.

Such, up to this point, is the story. But what came next? [?] Again I am compelled to cry out. Forgive me as I cry out over the grief. O Thrace, name to be shunned! O unhappy land, a nation known for its calamities! You who were once ravaged by enemy fire in the incursions of the barbarians, and now have received within yourself the very sum of the common calamity! From there the good is snatched away; there envy ran riot against the empire; there the shipwreck of the world took place; there, as though striking a reef in a heavy sea, we sank into the depth of sorrow. O that evil journey, which did not grant a return! O bitter waters, whose springs she drank as she ought not to have done! O place where the suffering happened, named for the moonless dark because of that suffering! For I hear that in their native tongue the place is called Scotumis. There the lamp was darkened, there the light was quenched, there the rays of the virtues grew dim. Gone is the adornment of the empire, the rudder of justice, the image of benevolence, or rather its very archetype. Taken away is the model of love for a husband, the pure offering of chastity, the approachable dignity, the gentleness that was never despised, the lofty humility, the candid modesty, the blended harmony of all good things. Gone is the zeal for the faith, the pillar of the Church, the ornament of the altars, the wealth of the poor, the right hand that sufficed for many, the common harbor of the oppressed. Let virginity mourn, let widowhood lament, let orphanhood wail; let them know what they had, now that they have it no longer. But why should I divide the lament into parts and ranks? Let the whole generation groan, sending up a deep groan from the midst of the heart. Let the priesthood itself share the grief too, since envy has robbed it of the ornament common to all. Would it be too bold to say the Prophet's words: "Why, O God, have you cast us off forever, and why has your wrath blazed against the sheep of your pasture?" For what sins are we paying the penalty? Why are we scourged with one calamity after another? Or perhaps, because the impiety of the various heresies has multiplied, this very sentence has prevailed against us? For you see what evils have befallen us in a short time. We had not yet recovered our breath after the first blow, we had not yet wiped the tears from our eyes, and again we have fallen into so great a calamity. Then we mourned the newly blooming flower; now we mourn the very stem from which the flower sprang. Then it was the beauty we had hoped for; now it is the beauty in its full prime. Then it was the good we expected; now it is the good we had known by experience. Will you forgive me, brothers, if in my grief I speak somewhat wildly? Perhaps, as the Apostle says, creation itself groaned together with us in our misfortune. Let me remind you of what happened, and I think most of you will agree with what I say. When the empress, covered with gold and purple, was

being brought into the city (a bier was what carried her, and every rank and every age had poured out of the city, and the open ground [?] was crowded by the multitude, all of them on foot, even those of the highest rank, escorting the procession of grief), you surely remember how the sun veiled its rays with clouds. Perhaps it did so in order not to see with its pure light the empress entering the city in such a guise: not on a chariot or a gold-mounted carriage, as befits imperial splendor, glorying in her guards, but covered in a coffin, her beauty hidden beneath a gloomy pall. It was a terrible and pitiable sight, set before all who met it as a cause of tears. All who had gathered, stranger and native alike, received her as she entered not with acclamations but with laments. Then the air too darkened in mourning, wrapping itself in gloom as in a mourning garment. And the clouds too, as far as they could, wept, letting fall soft drops upon the grief in place of tears. Or is this really nonsense, not even worth saying? For if anything of the kind happened in creation to mark the calamity, it surely came not from creation but from the Master of creation, who by what he did honored the death of this holy woman. For "precious," it says, "in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones." But I saw then another sight more wondrous than those I have mentioned. I saw a double rain streaming down upon the earth, one from the air and the other of tears, and the shower from the eyes was no less than that from the clouds. For among all those myriads present there was no eye that did not drench the earth with drops of tears. But perhaps we have not guessed the teacher's mind correctly, and have dwelt longer than we should on gloomy things. Perhaps he wishes to heal the hearers rather than distress them, and we have now done the opposite, like a physician who took charge of a wounded man and not only neglected to treat him but even rubbed corrosive drugs into the sufferer. So we must pour soothing speech like oil upon the swollen wound. For the healing of the Gospel too knows how to mix oil with the astringency of wine. Let us pour it upon you, then, taking the flask of oil from Scripture, and so far as we can let us recant the gloom of what has been said and turn it into consolation. But let no one disbelieve what I am about to say, even if it is surprising. The good which we seek, brothers, exists; it exists and has not perished. Or rather, I have said less than the truth. For not only does the good exist, but it now dwells in loftier places than before. Do you seek the empress? She lives in the royal palace. But do you long to see this

with your own eyes? You are not permitted to pry into the sight of an empress. Fearsome is the guard of the soldiers around her. I do not mean those guards whose weapon is iron, but those armed with the flaming [?], whose form human eyes cannot bear [?]. The hidden halls of the kingdom are among them, and you will see them when you too step out of the body. For there is no other way to enter the inner sanctuaries of the kingdom than by parting the curtain of the flesh. Or do you think it better to share in life by way of the flesh? Then let the divine Apostle teach you, who shared in the ineffable mysteries of paradise. What does he say about life here, perhaps speaking with the common voice of humankind? "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?" Why do you say this? Because to depart and be with Christ, he says, is far better. And what of [?] the great David, who abounded in so much power and had everything at his command for pleasure and enjoyment? Does he not feel cramped by life? Does he not call life here a prison? Does he not cry to the Lord, "Bring my soul out of prison"? Is he not vexed at the lengthening of life, saying, "Woe is me, that my sojourn is prolonged!"? Or did the saints not know how to tell the good from the worse, and was it for this reason that they thought departure from the body preferable for the soul? But you, tell me, what good do you see in life? Consider what life is made of. I will not quote to you the prophet's words, "All flesh is grass," for by that comparison he rather dignifies the wretchedness of our nature. Perhaps it would be better to be grass than to be what it is. Why? Because grass has nothing unpleasant in its nature, while our flesh is a workshop of stench, turning everything it takes in to corruption and uselessness. And to be subject all our lives to the service of the belly: what punishment is not less grievous than that? For look at this perpetual tax-collector, I mean the belly, and how great a demand it makes upon us every day! Even if we sometimes pay it in advance more than the appointed amount, nothing

[?] nor can we be in it either when we wish or for as long as we desire; we are brought in without knowing how, and we are moved out when we do not know. And you will understand the riddle of the jar if you look at how insatiable desires are. You see how people pour honors, powers, glories and all such things into themselves; but what is poured in leaks away and does not stay with the one who has it. For the eagerness for glory and power and honor is always at work, yet the jar of desire remains unfilled. And what of avarice? Is it not truly a pierced jar, leaking through its whole bottom, which, even if you pour the whole sea into it, by its nature [cannot] be filled [?]

What, then, is there to grieve over, if the blessed woman has been parted from the evils of life? Casting off the filth of the body like a speck of rheum from the eye, she passes with a pure soul to the undefiled life. There deceit has no citizenship, slander finds no belief, flattery has no place, and falsehood is not mixed in; pleasure and pain, fear and boldness, poverty and wealth, slavery and lordship, and all such unevenness of life are banished as far as possible from that life. "Sorrow and grief and sighing have fled away from there," as the prophet says. And in their place, what? Freedom from passion, blessedness, estrangement from every evil, the company of angels, the contemplation of things invisible, participation in God, joy without end. Should we then grieve over the empress, when we have learned what she has received [?] in exchange for what? She has left an earthly kingdom, but has gained the heavenly one. She has laid aside the crown of stones, but has put on the crown of glory. She has taken off the purple, but has put on Christ. This is the truly royal and precious garment. I hear that the purple here is dyed with the blood of a certain sea-snail, but the purple above is made to shine by the blood of Christ. You see how great a difference there is in the garment. Do you want to be convinced that she is among those above? Read the Gospel: "Come, you who are blessed by my Father" (the Judge says this to those on his right), "inherit the kingdom prepared for you." Prepared by whom? "Which you prepared for yourselves," he says, "by your works." How? "I was hungry, I was thirsty, I was a stranger, naked, sick, in prison... Inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me." If, then, zeal for these things wins the kingdom, count, if it is even possible to count, how many were clothed in garments from her! How many were fed by that great right hand! How many prisoners were granted not only a visit but full release! And if visiting a prisoner wins the kingdom, then setting him free from punishment is plainly worthy of greater honor, if there is anything higher than a kingdom. But her praise does not stop there. For it goes beyond even what is laid down for good deeds.

How many came to know through her, in their own persons, the grace of resurrection! Men who had died by the laws and received the sentence of death were called back to life again through her. The testimony to what I say is before your eyes. You saw the young man beside the altar despairing of his life. You saw the poor woman lamenting her brother's condemnation, as the one who proclaims good tidings to the Church announced how, in memory of the empress, the grim sentence of death is undone into life. Are these her only deeds? And where shall we place her humility, which Scripture ranks above every virtuous achievement? She shared the reins of so vast an empire with the great emperor; every power bowed down to her, so many nations paid her tribute, and land and sea each escorted her with its own riches. Yet she gave pride no hold over her, always [?] looking to herself and not to what lay outside herself. For this reason she becomes heir to the beatitude, having purchased true loftiness through humility in this passing life. Shall I give a proof of her love for her husband as well? When their bodily union was dissolved, the precious goods that belonged to her had of course to be divided too. How, then, did she make the division? There were three children (for these are the chief of all goods). She left the sons to their father, to be the supports of his empire, and as her own share she claimed only the daughter. Do you see how grateful and affectionate she was, yielding to her husband the greater part of what was precious? But I will add what most needs to be said by us, and then end my speech. Hatred of idols is common to all who share the faith; but her special distinction was to loathe the Arian unbelief as much as idolatry. For she held that those who think the Divine is among created things are no less worshippers of the creature than those who make idols out of matter, and she judged this rightly and piously. For whoever worships a creature, even if he does so in the name of Christ, is an idolater, giving the idol the name of Christ. Therefore, having learned that there is no new God, she worshipped one Godhead, glorified in Father and Son and Holy Spirit. In this faith she grew, in this she flourished, in this she committed her spirit to God. By this faith she was brought to the bosom of Abraham, the father of faith, beside the spring of paradise (whose drops do not reach the unbelievers), under the shade of the tree of life that is planted by the streams of waters. May we too be found worthy of these things in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory forever.
